title: Solar power is becoming bigger than nuclear
titleZh: Solar power is becoming bigger than nuclear
author: geox
relevanceReason: 命中 3 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: 1 day agoJocelyn TimperleyGetty Images(Credit: Getty Images)After defying projections, solar's dramatic growth means it is now overtaking nuclear as a global power source. Here are seven reasons for solar's success, and where it might go from here.The world's solar power is crossing a threshold. A decade ago, it barely registered on a global scale, providing just 1% of the world's power. In 2026, it will almost certainly increase to 10% of power, and overtake nuclear, a mainstay of electricity since the late 1970s."[Solar] generating more electricity than all the world's nuclear power plants is a pretty insane stat, for sure," says Dave Jones, co-founder of Ember. From China's vast arrays to a recent solar upsurge driven by escalating oil prices, the incredible rise of solar power has defied all projections. Here are seven ways it has become an apparently "unstoppable force" – and what the future looks like from here.1. An underestimated force "Solar is now the engine of the power transition," says Jan Rosenow, a professor of energy and climate policy at the University of Oxford in the UK.Solar has become the fastest-growing source of new electricity in history, and by far the largest source of new electricity globally. In 2025, it met three-quarters of the growth in the world's demand for electricity, overtaking wind power generation (wind power is also growing, just a little more slowly).That's where solar's going, to not just be king of electricity, but king of energy – Dave JonesEmber/ BBCEmber data shows solar electricity generation narrowly surpassing nuclear in 2025. In 2026, it will almost certainly well exceed it (Credit: Ember/BBC)2. 'Offensively cheap'In particular, a large fall in the price of panels in 2023-24 pushed us into the current era of what Jones calls "offensively cheap" solar. "A panel in itself is just so unbelievably cheap," he says. "It's well under $100 (£75)… and that's going to keep you generating electricity for 30, 40 years without any input at all."3. Global uptakeChina is still the world's biggest solar power by far but is by no means the only player."Tariffs and other federal policies that constrain renewable energy growth are certainly expected to raise costs and slow expansion relative to what we otherwise would have seen," says Alicia Zhao, an expert in US mitigation pathways at the University of Maryland. "However, economics are a key part of why solar has been able to grow so quickly. Even with rising costs, solar is still one of the cheapest sources of new power in the US. And it is getting built regardless of political lines."Getty ImagesChina's internal solar boom is now slowing down, but its cheap solar exports to other countries are still increasing (Credit: Getty Images)In Australia, over four million homes now have rooftop solar: well over a third of all households.4. Unreliable fossil fuels"What's really incredible in Pakistan is… generally most of the solar boom has been out of people's pockets," says Jones. "People can afford it, without needing to take out loans."A similar story has been seen in several other "sun belt" countries, from Lebanon to Nigeria. "[Solar] lets households act without waiting for governments or utilities," says Rosenow. "In uncertain times, that speed and independence is extremely valuable."5. Battery revolutionSolar power, of course, can only be produced during the day when the sun is shining. To turn it into electricity that can be dispatched at any time, it needs to be paired with batteries.Fortunately, batteries have been having their own cost revolution, transforming their ability to support the solar rollout. "Solar plus storage is now routinely cheaper than new fossil plants in sunny regions," says Rosenow. "Batteries have largely solved the daily problem of shifting midday sun into the evening."AlamySolar has gone from Pakistan's fifth-largest electricity source in 2023 to its largest in 2025, says Rosenow (Credit: Alamy)Barriers still remain for longer-term storage of solar across seasons, cloudy periods and monsoon seasons, though, both Rosenow and Jones say. It means the integration of solar into the wider electricity system still matters, says Rosenow.6. Electrify everything"That's where solar's going, to not just be king of electricity, but king of energy," says Jones. Still, it all requires a plan, Julia Souder, chief executive of the Long Duration Energy Storage Council, a global executive-led non-profit established at COP26, warned recently. "There is an inherent danger in uncontrolled electrification, and adding massive new loads without built-in flexibility creates a fragile system," she wrote in a blog for international policy network Ren21. "Electrification is not automatically resilient." The limits on solar are now grids, storage and how fast we electrify demand, says Rosenow – not panels or cost. "The bigger question is no longer whether solar grows but whether our power systems and institutions can keep up."In the US, data centres and electrification mean power demand is growing for the first time in decades, says Zhao, with energy security a national priority. "Renewables already make up over 90% of new capacity in the US," she says. "This need for secure, quickly deployable electricity could create a critical opportunity for [further] renewable energy growth even without support from the current federal government."7. Expanding techThey have now been approved in several other countries and US states including California.Meanwhile, agrivoltaics, which combines food production and solar panels, is being touted as a solution to concerns in some areas about the land use of solar.Getty ImagesIn Kentucky, US, a solar ranch pays a local farmer to graze his sheep among its solar panels, producing pasture-fed meat while keeping grass and weeds down (Credit: Getty Images)What's next for solarIn 2026, the world's solar capacity will go on rising, but the rate of expansion may slow down for the first time ever, says Jones.This is down to China: last summer, it changed its regime for managing and supporting new solar installations, leading to a burst of installations in 2025 to fall under the old price regime. Elsewhere, it's a different picture. "If you exclude China, there's more panels being installed this year than last year," says Jones."Wherever grid power is costly and unreliable, the economics keep pulling people towards solar," says Rosenow. "There is one caveat: if Chinese solar panels are difficult to import this will not happen at speed." More like this:But the solar success story shows we are also making progress in ways that were never anticipated. A decade ago, "no one was getting close to expecting that to happen", says Jones, noting that the growth in clean electricity has directly translated to fewer coal plants being built. --For more science, technology, environment and health stories from the BBC, follow us on Facebook and Instagram.

comments.author: zhivota
comments.textRawHtml:
Unregistered solar is huge in the developing world. In the Philippines, basically no one tells the utility they installed solar, because the net metering application is so expensive, comes with tons of red tape (read as opportunities for government officials to extract bribes), and only gives you billing credits anyway. So people just install batteries and automatic transfer switches. Some even disconnect from the grid completely, or never connect in the first place because it was too expensive to get the line installed. Automatic transfer to a generator is now very simple, and with LPG generators, extremely clean and low maintenance.

As I understand it, this is very common across much of the developing world now. So the tracking of how much solar energy there is in the world is almost certainly a lower bound on the reality.

children.author: fallingbananna
children.textRawHtml:
Even in the developed world, you don't need to register solar instalation as long as you don't plan to plug it into the general network, right?

If you have your own circuit with solar and battery and devices disconnected from the rest of the grid, then there is nothing to register, right?

children.author: lompad
children.textRawHtml:
For germany:

For balcony panels you only have to do a very small registration, but no large bureaucratic process or getting a permit.

For larger ones you still must get a permit for a very simple reason: even if you don't get your power into the general network, you still affect it by using less, which might cause issues with grid stability.

We have so much power on sunny days now that we can barely deal with it. Which in turn occasionally even causes power prices to go negative - you can get paid for drawing power.

children.author: MakersF
children.textRawHtml:
Dealing with power from solar panels is easy: you disconnect them (curtailment). So it's not a problem.

Have you ever wondered how is it possible that the price goes negative? Why would someone pay you to use the energy they produce? Logically, the price shouldn't go below 0 (*) . The reason is that the government gives incentives for each kWh produ ed. So if they pay you 0.10€/kWh, you'll be happy to pay people up to 0.09€/kWh as long as you can keep producing, since your marginal cost is 0. Basically government incentives are producing this situation, paying people to produce electricity nobody wants. It's also the reason why production is far from consumption: the incentives never were designed to push to generate useful electrons, just electrons, even if they cannot be moved to where they are useful. We need to rework how incentives are provided, because this is ending up wasting a ton of public money!

(*) except for power stations were they cannot physically turn it off, but generally they wouldn't be able to produce enough energy to define the marginal price

children.author: flakeoil
children.textRawHtml:
In that case the government should pay incentives when purchasing an electric car. That way the electricity being produced on sunny days can be stored and used when it is cloudy. Electric cars will also be spread out geographically, quite in line with solar panel installations so that solves for regional and network issues too. And as an added benefit we use less oil (less combustion cars) and less gas (we charge when it is sunny and not when we produce electricity with gas generators).

By using less oil and less gas we reduce CO2 emmissions, save money and are less dependent on other regions far away.
children.textZhHtml:
在这种情况下，政府应该在购买电动汽车时给予奖励。这样，晴天产生的电力就可以储存起来，阴天时也可以使用。电动汽车也将在地理上分布，与太阳能电池板的安装非常一致，这样也可以解决区域和网络问题。另外一个好处是，我们使用更少的石油（更少的燃油汽车）和更少的天然气（我们在阳光明媚的时候充电，而不是在使用燃气发电机发电时充电）。

通过使用更少的石油和天然气，我们减少了二氧化碳排放，节省了资金，并减少了对遥远其他地区的依赖。

children.textRawHtml:
I wonder if the excess energy could be used to do things like run carbon capture (although I've read that this is very much a pipe dream, that it'll take several magnitudes more carbon capture facilities to counter what we're currently producing).

In a very tiny Canary Island, their battery is many many tonnes of water pumped uphill when they have windpower: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RXhAj5BHdfM
children.textZhHtml:

在一个非常小的加那利群岛，他们的电池是当他们有风力发电时将许多吨的水抽上山：https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RXhAj5BHdfM

children.author: zarzavat
children.textRawHtml: This doesn’t make any sense. You also use less electricity if you switch off your devices. I think Germans just have a fetish for permits.
children.textZhHtml: 这没有任何意义。如果关闭设备，您的用电量也会减少。我认为德国人只是迷恋许可证。

children.author: leonidasrup
children.textRawHtml:
Adherence to regulations is one of the reasons why the German grid is so reliable.

The Germans manage their electric grid very well, the last major electric blackout in Germany was in 2006. (More than 15 million clients of the Union for the Co-ordination of Transmission of Electricity (UCTE) did not have access to electricity for about two hours on this date.)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_European_blackout

On the other hand electric grids in Philippines are quite unreliable and economic losses caused by blackouts are quite high:

" That is a brutal reminder that every blackout doesn’t just kill the lights; it sets the nation’s money, productivity, and economic progress on fire. " https://mb.com.ph/2026/10/26/blackouts-heavy-price-tag-is-ga...
children.textZhHtml:
遵守法规是德国电网如此可靠的原因之一。

德国人对电网管理得很好，德国上一次大停电是在 2006 年。（当天超过 1500 万电力传输协调联盟 (UCTE) 客户大约两个小时没有用上电。）

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_European_blackout

菲律宾的电网相当不可靠，停电造成的经济损失相当高：

" 这残酷地提醒我们，每次停电不仅会毁掉灯光，还会毁掉灯光。它点燃了国家的金钱、生产力和经济进步。 ” https://mb.com.ph/2026/10/26/blackouts-heavy-price-tag-is-ga...

children.author: lompad
children.textRawHtml: Regarding reliability: Absolutely. I honestly didn't experience a major blackout in my entire life in germany. I always forget just how big of a problem that still is for many countries and areas.
children.textZhHtml: 关于可靠性：绝对。老实说，我在德国的一生中没有经历过大停电。我总是忘记这对许多国家和地区来说仍然是一个多么大的问题。

children.author: lompad
children.textRawHtml:
On grid-scale this very much has an influence. Obviously not on individual scale. Is the influence big enough to warrant needing permits? Not sure, but I certainly see the problem.

In many areas solar panels get turned of by grid operators remotely for many hours on sunny days. In an area in the south I worked in around 50-70% of the produced power of larger installations (>30kwp) is essentially thrown away because the grid simply doesn't have enough capacity.
children.textZhHtml:
在网格规模上，这有很大的影响。显然不是在个人尺度上。影响力是否大到足以需要许可证？不确定，但我确实看到了问题所在。

在许多地区，电网运营商在阳光明媚的日子里会远程关闭太阳能电池板几个小时。在我工作过的南部地区，大型装置（>30kwp）的发电量大约有 50-70% 基本上被丢弃了，因为电网根本没有足够的容量。

children.author: zarzavat
children.textRawHtml:
Every day people go to work and turn off their electrical devices. Switching your home to off-grid solar + batteries is just like going to work and not coming back. The grid can handle it.

If many houses install off-grid solar, it's still not going to have a negative effect on the grid because the change is spread out over time.

It does mean that less generating capacity is needed over the long term, but decision makers can just get that data directly from the grid. I don't see what extra information the permit is adding.
children.textZhHtml:
人们每天上班都会关闭电子设备。将您的家改用离网太阳能+电池就像去上班而不回来一样。电网可以处理它。

如果许多房屋安装离网太阳能，它仍然不会对电网产生负面影响，因为这种变化会随着时间的推移而分散。

这确实意味着长期需要更少的发电量，但决策者可以直接从电网获取数据。我没有看到许可证添加了哪些额外信息。

children.author: gosub100
children.textRawHtml: It could be for fire code compliance. Not everyone knows that too much current through a small wire creates heat.
children.textZhHtml: 这可能是为了符合消防规范。并不是每个人都知道通过细电线的电流过多会产生热量。

children.author: leonidasrup
children.textRawHtml:
Every wire, small or large, has a maximum current which can safely pass through. Circuit breakers are used prevent overloading of power lines and potential fire.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circuit_breaker
children.textZhHtml:
每根电线，无论大小，都有一个可以安全通过的最大电流。 使用断路器可防止电线过载和潜在火灾。

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circuit_breaker

children.author: gosub100
children.textRawHtml: That's patronizing. My point is that electrical code requires the use of safety devices (breakers are only one). Idiots plugging wires together without oversight cause fires.
children.textZhHtml: 这太傲慢了。我的观点是，电气规范要求使用安全装置（断路器只是其中之一）。白痴在没有监督的情况下将电线插在一起会导致火灾。

children.author: michaelbuckbee
children.textRawHtml:
Yeah, if you're seen the recent rise in "balcony solar" it's more or less this.

People putting a couple panels up on their patio or whatever and having it charge one of those cooler sized batteries that they then run a few of their devices off of.

I've been thinking about a similar situation for my shed as I'd realized that the entire system would be cheaper than getting a line trenched to it.
